# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway was born in Mount Vernon, New York, on January 2, 1938. Initially experiencing gender dysphoria as a boy, she withdrew from MIT in 1959 and later resumed education at Columbia University's School of Engineering and Applied Science, earning her B.S. and M.S.E.E. degrees in 1962 and 1963. She was recruited by IBM Research in 1964, where she contributed to the Advanced Computing Systems (ACS) project, inventing multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling, which the Computer History Museum considers the first "superscalar" design.
After completing her gender transition in 1968 and adopting a new identity, Conway began her career as a contract programmer. She joined Xerox PARC in 1973, where she co-founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology. Collaborating with Ivan Sutherland and Carver Mead, she co-authored *Introduction to VLSI Systems* , a standard textbook in chip design. Conway invented dimensionless, scalable design rules and institutionalized the Metal Oxide Semiconductor Implementation Service (MOSIS) system in 1981, which greatly simplified chip design and fostered the growth of the electronic design automation industry. Later, she worked at DARPA before joining the University of Michigan in 1985.
